# Reconstructing Gilgit-Baltistan’s population change, 1951–2025

**Research review and portfolio foundation · Evidence checked 27 October 2026 · Study endpoint: 2025**

Gilgit-Baltistan’s official statistical compilations describe a population rising from approximately a quarter of a million in 1951 to **1,709,049 in the yearbook’s 2023 census table**. That broad increase is well supported, but a precise, continuous 1951–2025 series is not yet defensible: the sources contain conflicting totals, changing geographic units, rounded historical values, and estimates presented alongside census results. Recent household surveys suggest smaller households and lower fertility point estimates, but their methods and reference periods require indicator-by-indicator comparison. **No observed 2025 population total was verified in this review.** The strongest student research project is therefore an auditable reconstruction of population benchmarks, paired with carefully harmonized demographic indicators and a transparent account of what remains unknown. The later website should make those distinctions visible rather than hide them behind a smooth population curve. Historical evidence comes from the supplied GB yearbook and an independently retrieved [AJ&K Statistical Year Book 2024, table 15.20](https://www.pndajk.gov.pk/uploadfiles/downloads/AJ%26K%20Statistical%20Year%20Book%202024%281%29.pdf).

A suitable project subtitle is **“Census benchmarks, demographic transition, and uncertainty in mountain-region data.”** The central question is: *What do population benchmarks and household surveys jointly reveal about Gilgit-Baltistan’s demographic change, and how sensitive are the conclusions to source versions, geographic definitions, and measurement methods?* This is a research question that a BS-level data science portfolio can answer substantially with public aggregate evidence, while leaving room for later microdata analysis.

## The sources support benchmarks, not an annual census series

This review combines the five supplied PDFs with targeted searches of official statistical publications, UNICEF documentation, and academic research. The supplied yearbook and investment report were text-extracted and examined closely for population tables, definitions, and related context. The two recent MICS reports were text-indexed and their relevant demographic and methodological sections examined; the 731-page survey report was not individually read page by page. Relevant pages of the image-only 2016–17 key findings report were visually inspected. Suspicious yearbook tables were also checked against page images so that source mistakes could be distinguished from extraction errors. This is a focused evidence review, not an exhaustive systematic literature review or independent re-enumeration.

The following source identifiers keep local evidence traceable. “PDF page” means the physical page counted from the beginning of the file; “printed page” means the report’s own page label. Public catalogues linked here identify publication families; the supplied files, not an assumed matching online download, are the evidence for the cited local tables.

| ID | Supplied publication | Role and key locations |
|---|---|---|
| Y | *Gilgit-Baltistan Statistical Year Book 2024*, 294 PDF pages | Regional and district population; PDF pp. 81–86 / printed pp. 59–64, tables 3.2–3.14. |
| I | *Unlocking Investment Opportunities in Gilgit Baltistan, Pakistan*, 2024, 119 PDF pages | Economic and policy context; PDF pp. 20, 59–60 and 74. |
| M16 | *Gilgit-Baltistan MICS 2016–17 Key Findings Report*, 26 PDF pages | Earlier household indicators; PDF pp. 7–8 and 16 / printed pp. 3–4 and 12. |
| M24K | *MICS 2024–25 Key Findings Report*, 38 PDF pages, title dated December 2025 | Accessible summary, with discrepancies requiring comparison to the full report. |
| M24F | *MICS 2024–25 Survey Findings Report*, 731 PDF pages, title dated December 2025 | Detailed definitions, sample design, estimates and uncertainty; table-specific locations below. |

The [GB Planning and Development downloads catalogue](https://www.pnd.gog.pk/pages/downloads) lists the investment report and recent MICS publications. UNICEF provides the [2016–17 report and key findings](https://www.unicef.org/pakistan/reports/multiple-indicator-cluster-survey-2016-17-report-and-key-findings-gilgit-baltistan), including a full report that supplements the supplied summary. Some other government-hosted PDFs were discoverable only through indexed text because direct retrieval failed. Those are useful leads and corroboration, but are not equivalent to a fully inspected original.

A census count, an official projection, and a sample-survey estimate answer different questions. A census aims to enumerate a defined population at a reference date. A projection applies assumptions to a baseline. MICS estimates characteristics of households and individuals from a probability sample. Publication year introduces another date: a report issued in 2025 can contain a 2023 census count, retrospective fertility estimates, or earlier administrative records. Every extracted observation therefore needs separate reference-year, publication-year, measurement-type and geographic-coverage fields.

This distinction also affects national comparisons. A retrieved UNdata table for Pakistan’s 2023 census explicitly excludes AJ&K and GB. That demonstrates the coverage of that particular table; it does **not** demonstrate that no census occurred in GB. The GB yearbook explicitly identifies its own 2023 census results. Any comparison with Pakistan must check whether the national denominator includes the region, rather than assume identical coverage across publications. ([UNdata coverage footnote](https://data.un.org/Data.aspx?d=POP&f=tableCode%3A26%3BsexCode%3A0%3BareaCode%3A0%3BcountryCode%3A586%3BrefYear%3A2023); [PBS report-release notice](https://www.pbs.gov.pk/release-of-national-and-provincial-census-reports-of-population-and-housing-census-2023-2/))

## The long-run increase is clear, while precise values need a version ledger

The table below is a **preliminary evidence reconstruction**, not a finalized harmonized dataset. Early values retain the approximate precision of official compilations. The independently retrieved AJ&K yearbook reports historical GB figures in millions to three decimals; the supplied GB yearbook reports thousands. Neither establishes, on its own, that the earliest enumerations covered exactly the same geography as later ones. Original early census tables and territorial definitions remain a priority.

| Reference year | Population evidence | Current interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| 1951 | Approximately 254,000; competing indexed GB compilation: 252,000 | 254,000 appears in Y table 3.13 and AJ&K table 15.20. Preserve the competing 252,000 version; original enumeration unresolved. |
| 1961 | Approximately 308,000 from separate official compilation | AJ&K table 15.20 supports 308,000. Y table 3.13 visibly prints “8” thousand; flag that source entry rather than silently replace it. |
| 1972 | Approximately 417,000 | Agreement between the two inspected official compilations; original coverage not audited. |
| 1981 | Approximately 575,000 | Same qualification. |
| 1998 | Approximately 884,000 | Same qualification; do not turn rounded thousands into an exact headcount. |
| 2017 | 1,492,924 in Y table 3.3; 1,492,685 in Y tables 3.2 and 3.7 | Two internally consistent source versions; neither adjudicated as the definitive revision. |
| 2022 | 1.7 million in I | Explicitly an estimate; useful policy context, not an additional census observation. |
| 2023 | 1,709,049 in Y table 3.3(a) | Exact figure reported in the yearbook’s census table; original underlying census volume not independently obtained. |
| 2025 | No observed total verified | Keep missing in an observed-count series. Any later projection must be separately labeled and documented. |

Historical references: Y PDF p. 86 / printed p. 64, table 3.13; [AJ&K yearbook](https://www.pndajk.gov.pk/uploadfiles/downloads/AJ%26K%20Statistical%20Year%20Book%202024%281%29.pdf), PDF p. 211 / printed p. 176, table 15.20. The competing early version appears in indexed text of [GB at a Glance 2020](https://portal.pnd.gog.pk/Content/Files/Reports/Gilgit%20Baltistan%20at%20a%20Glance%20New%20Design%202020%20Final_210554160.pdf), whose direct retrieval failed. Recent references: Y PDF pp. 81–84 / printed pp. 59–62; I PDF pp. 59 and 74. The historical and district JSON files accompanying this report preserve source observations rather than proclaim a final canonical series.

Using the yearbook’s table 3.3 version, the reported population increase between 2017 and 2023 is **216,125 people, or 14.48%**. Using its alternative 2017 total produces **216,364 people, or 14.49%**. These are analyst calculations from the source values, not new observations. With a simplified six-year interval, the compound annual growth rate rounds to **2.28% under either version**: `100 × [(P2023 / P2017)^(1/6) − 1]`. Exact-date calculations should replace that convention if census reference dates become available. The regional finding is robust to this small discrepancy, but silently mixing versions would make the work irreproducible.

The inconsistency is more consequential when analysing components. Different yearbook tables report different male, female and transgender totals for 2017, and their district differences do not all have the same sign. A source cannot be “corrected” by adjusting only the regional sum. Similarly, table 3.2 prints an urban total that disagrees with its components; table 3.7 supplies a reconciling total. Table 3.14 duplicates an age band and contains problematic percentages. An age pyramid made directly from that table would therefore need validation before publication. These are visibly printed issues, not merely OCR failures. [Source Y: tables 3.2, 3.7 and 3.14; PDF pp. 81, 84 and 86 / printed pp. 59, 62 and 64.]

A separate projection trap appears in Y table 3.4: **1,748,769** is printed under an adjacent “Population (P)” heading whose year alignment is ambiguous. The table’s density uses that projected numerator rather than the reported census total. It should not be labeled “2025 population” without clarification. Similarly, the investment report’s rounded 1.7 million for 2022 cannot be compared mechanically with 1,709,049 for 2023 to infer stagnation. Their measurement basis, rounding and reference years differ. [Source Y: PDF p. 82 / printed p. 60; source I: PDF pp. 59, 74.]

District data are nevertheless valuable. The following reproduces the table 3.3 version alongside table 3.3(a), preserving the yearbook’s ten-unit reporting structure. Differences are arithmetic comparisons only: **boundary consistency and census coverage must be established before interpreting these as district growth or migration rankings**.

| Reporting district | 2017, version A | 2023 | Arithmetic difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Astore | 95,416 | 111,573 | 16,157 |
| Diamer | 269,772 | 337,329 | 67,557 |
| Ghanche | 156,697 | 157,822 | 1,125 |
| Ghizer | 172,696 | 200,069 | 27,373 |
| Gilgit | 285,236 | 324,552 | 39,316 |
| Hunza | 51,372 | 65,497 | 14,125 |
| Kharmang | 54,613 | 61,304 | 6,691 |
| Nagar | 71,746 | 87,410 | 15,664 |
| Shigar | 74,540 | 84,608 | 10,068 |
| Skardu | 260,836 | 278,885 | 18,049 |
| **GB total** | **1,492,924** | **1,709,049** | **216,125** |

Source Y, PDF p. 82 / printed p. 60; differences calculated for this review. The alternative 2017 district version is preserved in the accompanying ledger. A historical geographic crosswalk must record names, dates, splits and merges. Where exact reallocation is impossible, aggregate to a stable larger unit or declare the comparison unavailable. Modern district polygons should not be joined retrospectively to 1951 totals merely because a name matches.

## Household surveys suggest transition, with important limits to comparison

MICS adds information that census totals alone cannot provide. The 2024–25 full report describes a two-stage stratified design with **357 clusters and 7,140 selected households**, of which **6,929 were interviewed**. Its geographic reporting domains include GB, urban/rural areas and ten survey districts. The 2016–17 key findings report records **6,213 interviewed households**. These sample sizes are not population totals. In particular, M24F’s normalized weighted count of **46,136 household members** must never be entered as GB’s population. [M24F sections 2.2 and SR.1.1, PDF pp. 21 and 48 / printed pp. 3 and 30; normalization and household composition, PDF pp. 56–59 / printed pp. 38–41; M16 PDF p. 7 / printed p. 3; public access through [UNICEF](https://www.unicef.org/pakistan/reports/multiple-indicator-cluster-survey-2016-17-report-and-key-findings-gilgit-baltistan) and [GB P&D](https://www.pnd.gog.pk/pages/downloads).]

Both newer reports carry December 2025 title dates, but their fieldwork descriptions differ slightly. The full report describes late September 2024 through late January 2025; the key findings introduction gives October–January, while its summary gives October–February. Record the discrepancy and preserve each statement rather than invent one exact common date. More importantly, survey fieldwork is not the reference period for every indicator: fertility and mortality estimates look back over specified windows. [M24F section 2.12, PDF p. 25 / printed p. 7; M24K PDF pp. 3 and 5.]

| Indicator | 2016–17 | 2024–25 | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Mean household size | 7.7 | 6.7 | Suggests smaller households; verify household and residence definitions before formal comparison. |
| Total fertility rate, children per woman | 4.6 | 4.2 | Lower point estimate, but old full-report table uses one preceding year and the new report uses three. |
| Adolescent birth rate, per 1,000 women aged 15–19 | 46.9 | 34.8 | Same reference-window problem; avoid treating the difference as a demonstrated annual decline. |
| Contraceptive prevalence, any method, currently married women aged 15–49 | 38.1% | 45.2% | Potentially comparable after checking coding, sampling and the eligible population. |
| Women aged 20–24 with a live birth before age 18 | 11.3% | 8.0% | Similar headline definition; verify the exact survey universes and uncertainty. |

References: M16 PDF pp. 7 and 16 / printed pp. 3 and 12; M24F SR.3.2 PDF p. 58 / printed p. 40, TM.1.1 PDF p. 98 / printed p. 80, and TM.2.2W/TM.3.1 indicator summary PDF p. 29 / printed p. 11. The older fertility window is documented in RH.2 of the [2016–17 full report](https://www.unicef.org/pakistan/media/3131/file/MICS%202016-17%20GB%20Full%20Report.pdf). These are survey estimates, not exact population parameters or evidence that every district follows the same trajectory.

The most defensible interpretation is that household composition and reproductive behaviour merit investigation as part of a demographic transition. Smaller households do not imply fewer people overall: household formation, living arrangements, migration and fertility all affect household size. Nor do two fertility estimates establish a continuous decline. The new report supplies a total fertility rate confidence interval of approximately **3.88–4.56** around its 4.2 estimate; a formal change test also requires the older estimate’s uncertainty and comparable windows. Overlapping or non-overlapping point estimates alone do not answer that question. [M24F Appendix C, SE.1, PDF p. 349 / printed p. 331.]

Mortality needs a stronger separation. The earlier key report gives infant mortality of **73.5** and under-five mortality of **91.8 per 1,000 live births**, based on an indirect Time Since First Birth method with a January 2015 reference. The new full report gives **43** and **50**, using direct full birth histories for the most recent five-year window. These values should be displayed with their methods and reference periods, not presented as a clean annual percentage reduction. The new survey also contains retrospective estimates for earlier windows, but those are estimates reconstructed from one survey, not independent historical surveys. [M16 PDF p. 8 / printed p. 4; M24F CS.1, PDF pp. 91–92 / printed pp. 73–74.]

The recent reports also disagree internally. M24K reports an under-five share of **15.0%** and an under-18 share of **50.4%**, while the detailed M24F household-population table gives **14.0%** and **48.3%**. Moreover, **17.4%** is the urban *household* share in the full report, although the key report labels it a population share. The detailed table can be a provisional analytic preference because it exposes its denominator, but the disagreement must remain visible until clarified. It is not legitimate to select whichever number best fits a demographic story. [M24K PDF p. 5 / printed p. ii; M24F SR.3.1 and SR.4.1, PDF pp. 57 and 59 / printed pp. 39 and 41.]

Education can contextualize these patterns only after equivalent indicators are identified. Literacy among young women, literacy among all adults, school completion, and foundational reading among children use different populations and instruments. Combining them into one “education improvement” line would create a false trend. Respondent-level analysis, if later available through approved access, should use survey weights, strata and clusters; ordinary unweighted means and simple-random-sample standard errors would misrepresent the design. The [IPUMS MICS user guide](https://mics.ipums.org/mics/user_guide.shtml) and [MICS methods paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6771654/) provide useful starting points. Availability of 2024–25 microdata was not confirmed here.

## Roads, migration and settlement change explain mechanisms, not causal shares

Population accounting starts with an identity: change equals births minus deaths plus net migration, with any change in boundaries or coverage accounted for separately. The identity is not a decomposition unless its components are measured adequately. The supplied yearbook contains civil-registration tables, but registered events need not equal events occurring within that year, and coverage and late registration have not been established. Subtracting raw registrations from intercensal change to “calculate migration” would therefore be unjustified. [Source Y: CRMS tables, PDF pp. 83–84 / printed pp. 61–62.]

The literature helps formulate mechanisms and observable hypotheses. Kreutzmann’s work on the Karakoram Highway links transport accessibility to the integration of mountain societies with wider economic and political systems. His settlement research in central Hunza adds land, irrigation, lineage and migrant settlements to the explanation. These studies show why demographic change should be analysed through settlement histories and connections between places, rather than a regional count alone. They do not identify a causal coefficient saying how much the highway increased GB’s population. ([Kreutzmann, 1991](https://lib.icimod.org/records/fmqwy-7m305); [Kreutzmann, 1996](https://doi.org/10.3112/erdkunde.1996.03.02))

Recent land-use research provides a feasible extension. Ali and colleagues examine selected sites in Ghizer, Hunza and Nagar and document changing land uses through mixed methods. A later Gilgit-city study combines land-cover analysis with expert interviews. These offer approaches for a focused urban case study, but selected urbanizing locations are not a representative sample of all GB, and built-up area is not itself a population measure. Housing, commercial development, tourism, infrastructure and seasonal occupancy can all change land cover without proportional changes in usual residents. ([Ali et al., 2022 volume](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10708-021-10478-3); [Shah et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1007/s44327-025-00113-y))

Migration should also be treated as more than a permanent move from one district to another. Educational migration, employment, return movement and multi-local livelihoods can coexist with population growth in the origin region. Qualitative work on Gojal after the Attabad landslide illustrates disrupted and restored mobility rather than a simple one-way displacement story. A small household study of internal migration offers hypotheses about housing and infrastructure, but its observational design and limited sample do not establish regional prevalence or causal effects. ([Sökefeld, 2014 issue](https://doi.org/10.15460/ethnoscripts.2014.16.1.785); [Ullah et al., 2024](https://ijciss.org/index.php/ijciss/article/view/922))

The investment report is useful here as a statement of policy priorities and proposed development opportunities. It discusses education and work-related movement, seasonal residence patterns, and infrastructure needs. It does not provide a validated migration series, and proposed project dates are not evidence that projects were completed. Treat tourism, energy, education and roads as contexts for research questions rather than explanations already proven by the report. [Source I: PDF pp. 20, 59–60 and 97–100; publication discoverable through [GB P&D](https://www.pnd.gog.pk/pages/downloads).]

Three testable propositions follow. First, broad regional growth should be relatively insensitive to the two 2017 source versions; the calculations above provisionally support that proposition. Second, district differences should persist after harmonizing boundaries and source versions; that remains untested and could fail if administrative changes explain apparent differences. Third, smaller households and lower fertility should remain visible after aligning survey definitions and accounting for uncertainty; that also remains untested. A highway or tourism causation claim would require an additional identification strategy and appropriate comparison data, beyond this descriptive project.

## A reproducible research package can become a credible website

The immediate contribution should be a documented dataset and analysis notebook, not a complex prediction model. With a sparse set of census benchmarks, interpolating every intervening year creates a much larger-looking table without adding independent observations. Fitting a flexible machine-learning model to those synthetic rows would risk learning the interpolation rule and presenting it as demographic evidence. A clear benchmark chart, source-sensitivity analysis and honest missing-data treatment are stronger results.

The data pipeline should retain immutable source copies, retrieval dates and file hashes; extract text with page boundaries; transcribe the relevant tables; and visually check ambiguous cells. Store raw values and units alongside normalized values. Each row should carry source ID, table, PDF and printed page, geographic name and vintage, reference year, publication year, measurement type, precision, verification status and conflict note. Version A and version B must remain separate records. A curated view can select one version under an explicit rule while the raw ledger preserves all alternatives.

Validation should test district sums against published totals, sex components against the stated universe, percentages against denominators, duplicate age bands, units, and impossible values. These tests should flag source issues rather than automatically replace them. A correction needs its own supporting source and decision record. The historical JSON supplied with this review contains six rounded official-compilation records; the district JSON contains thirty observations across the two 2017 versions and 2023. They are starting evidence ledgers, **not a completed boundary-harmonized dataset**.

Analysis can then proceed in a limited sequence: benchmark change and source sensitivity; boundary-checked district comparisons; household-indicator comparisons with definitions and uncertainty; and, only as an optional appendix, a transparent constant-growth extension to 2025. Such an extension would use a stated baseline and rate assumption, show alternative assumptions, and carry a “scenario, not observed population” label. It should not appear as the headline 2025 result, and different assumed growth rates are not statistical confidence intervals. A cohort-component projection would require age-sex, fertility, survival and migration inputs that this review has not validated.

The website can later expose four connected views: a benchmark timeline with distinct census and projection markers; a district comparison using a verified boundary vintage; a household-indicator panel with comparability flags; and a source-audit page containing the discrepancies and decisions. Each chart should identify its source table, reference period, units and status. Missing years should remain visibly missing. A map is optional until appropriate boundaries are obtained; a clear table is preferable to a geographically misleading map.

Before a definitive public analysis, the highest-value unresolved work is obtaining the original early enumeration tables, asking the GB statistical authority which 2017 version is authoritative, confirming the meaning and year of the adjacent projection, obtaining boundary documentation, and resolving the recent MICS summary/full-report inconsistencies. These requests have not been sent. Further access to survey microdata would enable weighted analyses, but the public aggregate evidence already supports a substantial first project. Gridded population products could be considered later only after product documentation, GB coverage and dependence on census inputs are checked; they should not be assumed to independently validate the census.

For a scholarship portfolio, describe the work accurately as **an evidence audit and reproducible demographic analysis**, supported by a versioned repository, transparent calculations, data dictionary and source-linked visualizations. A portfolio statement can explain what you found, what you could reproduce, and where you declined to overclaim. Open Doors programme requirements and eligibility were not investigated in this review, and no admissions outcome can be inferred from the project. Its academic value lies in demonstrating statistical judgment: identifying meaningful patterns while preserving the uncertainty and limitations that make those patterns trustworthy.
